q: A patient has had a TIA with 75% ipsilateral carotid stenosis. When should carotid endarterectomy ideally take place?
o: Only if a second TIA occurs
why: The risk of stroke is highest soon after a TIA, so referral is within 24 hours and surgery ideally within 2 weeks for symptomatic 50–69% or over 70% stenosis.

q: What did the GALA trial show when comparing GA with local anaesthesia for carotid endarterectomy?
o: No significant difference in stroke, MI or death at 1 year
GA had shorter length of stay
why: GALA found similar outcomes (stroke, MI, death, length of stay) between GA and LA; a later meta-analysis suggested fewer haematomas with regional techniques.

q: What is the main advantage of performing carotid endarterectomy awake under regional anaesthesia?
o: No need for an arterial line
Lower rate of phrenic nerve palsy
why: An awake patient is the best neurological monitor during clamping; it also avoids airway instrumentation and may reduce shunt use.

q: Where is a deep cervical plexus block performed?
o: Along a line from the mastoid to C6, at C2–C4 transverse processes
At the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid only
At the angle of the mandible
why: C2, C3 and C4 lie about 2, 3 and 4 cm below the mastoid on the line to C6 (cricoid level). The superficial block is along the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid.

q: Which is a recognised complication of a deep cervical plexus block?
why: Complications include phrenic nerve palsy, haematoma, LA toxicity, subarachnoid or intravascular injection, infection and nerve injury.

q: Under GA, which technique can be used to monitor cerebral perfusion during carotid clamping?
o: Transcranial Doppler of the middle cerebral artery
why: Options include stump pressure, NIRS, transcranial Doppler of the MCA, and EEG.

q: Ten days after carotid endarterectomy a hypertensive patient presents with a severe ipsilateral headache and seizures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Hyperperfusion syndrome (1–3%) follows loss of autoregulation after relief of stenosis; it can occur up to a month after surgery and is treated with tight BP control.

q: An hour after carotid endarterectomy, a patient has a rapidly enlarging neck swelling and stridor. What is the immediate priority?
o: Open the wound to decompress the haematoma and secure the airway
Wait for the surgeon to arrive
why: A neck haematoma can rapidly obstruct the airway: open the wound to decompress it, call for help and secure the airway.

q: After carotid endarterectomy, a patient’s BP is labile, swinging between hypertension and hypotension. What is the most likely cause?
o: Baroreceptor dysfunction from carotid sinus manipulation
why: Carotid sinus manipulation and baroreceptor damage cause post-op hypertension or hypotension; monitor in HDU.

q: Which cranial nerve injury is a recognised complication of carotid endarterectomy?
why: Cranial nerve injuries include the facial (marginal mandibular branch, VII) and hypoglossal (XII) nerves, as well as recurrent laryngeal injury.
